one_liner: One-commit Node benchmark: a Rust Collatz loop compiled to wasm runs 45.6x faster than a naive JS loop and 6.5x faster than an ffi-napi call.
what_it_does: This is a benchmark repository, not a library. It implements one Collatz step counter three ways (plain JavaScript, a Rust cdylib called through ffi-napi, and Rust built with wasm-pack --target nodejs) and times them with Benchmark.js on input 670617279. The reusable part is a template: a `#[wasm_bindgen] pub fn collatz_steps(n: u64) -> u64` plus a three-line CommonJS wrapper that converts the Number argument to a BigInt.
how_it_is_fast: The wasm module runs the loop on 64-bit integers. The JavaScript loop's values climb to 966,616,035,460 (986 steps, 370 of them odd; derived by recomputing the sequence), far beyond the int32/Smi range, so V8 runs the % 2 and / 2 on float64 numbers. That works out to about 31.5 ns per step versus 0.69 ns for wasm. Against FFI, the gain is per-call overhead, not code quality: ffi-napi marshals every call through libffi and ref-napi (its own README warns of 'non-trivial overhead associated with FFI calls'), costing 4.43 us per call versus 0.68 us for the whole wasm call including BigInt conversion.
when_to_use: As a template for moving a hot integer kernel from Node.js JavaScript into Rust/wasm-bindgen when it needs exact 64-bit integer math that JS can only do with float64 or BigInt.
Kernels doing roughly a microsecond or more of work per call with scalar arguments, so the BigInt conversions at the JS/wasm boundary are amortised.
Deciding between ffi-napi and wasm for a small Rust function called at high frequency: with little work per call, wasm's in-process call beats ffi-napi's dynamic marshalling.
A minimal wasm-pack --target nodejs setup that loads synchronously with require().
when_not_to_use: As evidence that wasm beats native code: the FFI row is dominated by ffi-napi's call path. A Node-API addon (napi-rs, node-addon-api) or a native loop doing many iterations per call was not tested.

As evidence against well-written JavaScript: the JS kernel was not adapted to float64. For example, testing parity with `n & 1` (ToInt32 keeps parity for any safe integer) avoids the float64 remainder. Not measured.
Workloads that pass strings, arrays or buffers across the boundary: only one integer in and one integer out was measured.
Browsers or bundlers: only a --target nodejs build is set up (webpack and @wasm-tool/wasm-pack-plugin are in devDependencies but unused).
When you need reproducible numbers: no CPU, OS or Node version, one run printed, a single commit and no CI.

integration.form: source-drop (example repo: a Rust crate built with wasm-pack --target nodejs plus a CommonJS wrapper)
integration.dependencies: wasm arm: wasm-bindgen 0.2.92; FFI arm: ffi-napi 4.0.3 and ref-napi 3.0.3 (native node-gyp builds); harness: benchmark 2.1.4, yargs 17.7.2
integration.min_toolchain: Rust (2021 edition) with wasm-pack, and a Node.js with BigInt and wasm i64 integration; exact versions not documented
integration.platforms: any Node.js platform for the wasm arm; the FFI arm needs the cdylib built per OS
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (pure function, no shared state)

gotchas: Return types differ: the wasm wrapper returns a BigInt and the JS version a Number. The harness's correctness check uses loose assert.equal (986 == 986n), which hides this; a strict check would fail, and callers must convert.

The README's five reasons why wasm beats FFI (runtime symbol resolution, better inlining, the linear memory model) are not measured, and the first is wrong for this code: ffi.Library() resolves collatz_steps once at load in ffi/collatz.js, so the per-call cost is libffi/ref-napi argument and return marshalling.

The FFI arm declares ['int64', ['int64']] over a signed i64 Rust function with assert!(n > 0), while the wasm arm is u64. The FFI wrapper does no input check of its own (only benchmark.js validates via yargs), so passing 0 makes Rust panic inside an extern "C" function, which Rust 1.81 and later turn into a process abort. The wasm arm traps instead.
The FFI baseline rests on ffi-napi 4.0.3 (released March 2021; last repository commit March 2022). A modern FFI module such as Koffi, which claims low overhead relative to Node-API, was not compared.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Within its category it is the smallest Rust/wasm-bindgen example and the only one with a native-FFI arm, while wasm-perf (Emscripten SIMD matrix multiply, about 23.5x over JS) and JavaScript-vs-WebAssembly-Comparative-Analysis exercise heavier kernels. For a fairer native baseline, iswasmfast (catalogued under wasm-libraries-and-apps) pits wasm against an N-API addon instead of ffi-napi.
verified_claims_summary: Author's Benchmark.js run in Node (CPU, OS and Node version not stated) on input 670617279, after one equality check of the step counts: JS 32,172 ops/s (31.1 us per call), Rust via ffi-napi 225,918 ops/s (4.43 us), Rust via wasm-bindgen 1,465,898 ops/s (0.68 us), so wasm is 45.6x JS and 6.5x FFI (derived from page data). The JS gap mostly reflects float64 arithmetic forced by values above 2^31; the FFI gap reflects ffi-napi call overhead.
status_note: Single commit on 2024-04-21, 10 stars, MIT; a frozen demo rather than a maintained project, fine to copy as a wasm-pack template, but its FFI arm depends on ffi-napi, which has had no release since 2021.
